extracted.intended_audience: dataset creators, data labelers, and ML researchers building/curating math word-problem datasets
extracted.subtask_description: Write simple grade-school-level math word problems and their step-by-step solutions for inclusion in a training/evaluation dataset (GSM8K). Includes requirements on arithmetic operations, solution format, diversity, and quality-control procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall goal / problem level
rubrics_metrics.description: Your goal in this project is to write simple grade school level math word problems and their corresponding solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce problems appropriate for grade-school reasoning (not requiring advanced math). The dataset target is to train language models to solve natural language math problems and measure reasoning ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of solution steps
rubrics_metrics.description: All problems should contain 2-8 steps in their solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design problems whose worked solutions naturally break into between two and eight distinct reasoning/calculation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple mental arithmetic only
rubrics_metrics.description: All calculations should be simple enough to do in your head without a calculator (e.g. 7*8, 36+110).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arithmetic that requires long multiplication, complex fractions, or heavy computation; use examples with small integers and mentally-evaluable operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final answer is a single integer
rubrics_metrics.description: The answer should be a single integer value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any units should be specified as part of the question (e.g. 'How much money, in dollars, does Robert have?'). Simple decimal numbers (e.g. 3.25) can appear in intermediate steps, but final answers should always be integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show calculations in solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing 'Jason has 8/2=4 apples' is preferable to writing 'Jason has 4 apples', if you used the calculation 8/2 to determine how many apples Jason has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explicit step-by-step arithmetic expressions in the worked solution so the chain of reasoning is visible to verifiers and models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only allow elementary arithmetic operations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include advanced operators, exponents beyond simple integers, algebraic manipulations requiring symbolic manipulation, or other non-elementary math.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify units in the question
rubrics_metrics.description: Any units should be specified as part of the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make unit expectations explicit in the question text to avoid ambiguity in the expected final answer format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reusing problem settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't reuse a problem setting. If you just wrote a problem about Samantha's trip to the zoo, don't write a second problem using that same premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate each problem scenario from scratch to maximize topical diversity and reduce near-duplicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure problem diversity via embedding-based de-duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate a sentence embedding for each problem statement, compute cosine similarity between problems, and discard all problems above a similarity threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use automated similarity measures (the OpenAI team also provided similarity measures) to identify and remove problems that are semantically too similar; example shows discarding near-duplicate shopping/price problem pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent ambiguous wording; clarify interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid subtle ambiguities in phrasing that create multiple natural interpretations leading to different answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay special attention to language that can be read multiple ways (example: blanket problem where it's unclear whether a blanket was already on the bed). Make questions explicit so only one reasonable interpretation exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification: double-solve and resolve disagreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask two Surgers to solve each problem, paying extra attention to the language, and double-check any problems where at least one of their answers differed from the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple independent solutions to catch errors and ambiguities; flag and review any discrepancies between solvers before including the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeler selection and onboarding
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer Surgers with math or STEM degrees; everyone's first 5 submissions were reviewed by another qualified Surger, and those whose problems passed were added to the team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select labelers with stronger quantitative backgrounds to reduce calculation errors and increase speed. Use a probationary review process (e.g., review the first N submissions) before adding contributors to the main team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use starter problems as inspiration but create from scratch
rubrics_metrics.description: OpenAI provided auto-generated 'starter problems' for inspiration, but because the problems often didn’t make sense and had to be substantially reworked, most Surgers found it easier to create problems from scratch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starter/generative prompts can help brainstorm, but be prepared to heavily edit or discard nonsensical auto-generated examples; prefer crafting clear, original problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, practical labeling instructions with real examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructions are fairly short. Real-world examples are worth their weight in gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep guidelines concise where possible — long instructions only when criteria are very nuanced. Include realistic, worked examples (not 'armchair' examples) so labelers understand expectations concretely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch and eliminate mathematical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that all problems have mathematically correct answers; as a first pass, ask Surgers to double-check their work for mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine individual self-checks with independent verification (see double-solve) and programmatic/unit checks where possible to remove calculation mistakes before dataset inclusion.
